title: Flight delay propagation and downstream prediction

slides.title: Random forest: August MAE 13.655 min
claims: RQ2: 560,077 final connections, RMSE 42.917 min
RQ1: 24/25 supported estimates show fewer delay minutes
Retrospective evidence, conditional on completed connections
slides.notes: The main prediction result is an August mean absolute error of 13.655 minutes for the frozen primary predictor, Random forest. Its root mean squared error is 42.917 minutes over 560,077 accepted connections. The airport analysis supports 25 estimates under the unchanged development reference. These are the two findings around which I will explain the project. A simple baseline was allowed to win, so model complexity is not a success criterion. The analysis is retrospective and describes valid observed completed connections. It does not assign causal responsibility to airports, and the final test result did not trigger another round of tuning.

slides.title: Prediction time and research questions
claims: RQ1: downstream minus upstream delay, with upstream delay ≥15 min
RQ2: downstream nonnegative departure delay, including upstream on-time flights
UTC forward validation, then one frozen August assessment
slides.notes: The first question describes how delay changes across consecutive flights of the same aircraft. For the main airport analysis, upstream delay must reach fifteen minutes and the connection must be nonovernight. A negative net change means fewer delay minutes downstream, even if the aircraft remains late. The second question predicts nonnegative downstream departure delay at upstream actual arrival. Its population includes upstream on-time flights, and eligibility requires the prediction time to precede the downstream departure label. Training uses only labels mature before each UTC validation boundary. The forward folds train through April, May and June and validate the following month. August remains the final frozen assessment.

slides.title: The prediction sample differs from all flights
claims: Development: 2,261,775 valid prediction connections
355 airports, 6,591 routes
437,491 overnight connections reported separately
slides.notes: The development prediction sample contains 2,261,775 valid connections across 355 airports and 6,591 routes. It includes 437,491 overnight connections, which receive separate error reporting. These counts describe connections, not the number of individual flights. Cleaning first follows scheduled same-tail order, then checks actual timing and endpoint continuity. Cancellations, diversions and ambiguous chains define exclusions rather than zero delay. This completed-connection selection limits operational interpretation because future completion is not guaranteed at prediction time. Planned schedule availability and static aircraft inventories also remain assumptions. Keeping these population definitions explicit prevents a lower error on a different sample from masquerading as an improvement.

slides.title: Support-selected airport examples
claims: 25 frozen airports, 25 supported final estimates
24 negative estimates; FLL interval includes zero
slides.notes: The development procedure froze 25 airports and 16 common master cells. The final main-threshold analysis supports 25 airport estimates, with standardized means spanning -16.424 to 0.436 minutes. Among supported point estimates, 24 are negative. The sole positive point estimate is FLL, plus 0.436 minutes, with 95% interval [-2.403, 3.012], which includes zero. Across the raw main population of 482,013 connections, the mean change is -7.254 minutes, which differs from standardized comparison. The standardization reuses the same airport set, cells and threshold-conditional pooled development weights. It does not renormalize separately for a weakly supported airport. Unsupported estimates remain missing. An airport may lose support in a particular month, so missing months stay NA rather than becoming zero or entering a rank. The April–August RQ1 summary includes development months and is not an independent August validation.

slides.title: Random forest wins the registered comparison
claims: Feature source R0017; learned model R0025
Frozen primary predictor: Random forest
slides.notes: The feature-selection decision retained R0017. The six tree and forest candidates then hold that feature set and preprocessing fixed. The chart includes four decision trees across two depths and two minimum-leaf sizes, plus two random forests at fixed depth. Forests use two hundred trees and one-half of features per split, with seed forty-two. The retained learned model is R0025, while the primary predictor is Random forest. The recorded reason is: Registered family minima and sequential practical/monthly-stability promotion, followed by minimum pooled MAE against all three baselines. The practical and monthly-stability promotion rule was committed after P3, before weather and tree results were inspected. It was not registered before P0. The chosen primary need not be the single lowest-error trial among every exploratory candidate.

slides.title: August evaluates the frozen primary and comparators
claims: Primary MAE 13.655 min, RMSE 42.917 min
560,077 connections in the UTC August test window
slides.notes: This is the final August comparison after the rules, features, preprocessing and primary predictor were frozen. The primary, Random forest, records MAE 13.655 minutes and RMSE 42.917 minutes. The table also preserves the learned model and all three simple comparators. The mean and median baselines are estimated from mature training labels, while carry-forward transfers upstream delay directly. MAE is the primary decision metric because it measures average absolute minutes. RMSE gives greater weight to large errors. Neither metric alone describes every delay regime. The 6 paired intervals are individual 95% intervals, not a joint 95% statement across comparisons. The final access ledger and saved-result verification identify this test. These slides read saved summaries only, without reopening test labels or refitting.

slides.title: Interpretation stays conditional on the fitted models
claims: Largest displayed permutation change: G1_upstream_delay, 14.951 min
Date-block intervals condition on fitted predictions and selection
Airport rankings, permutation and PDP are noncausal
slides.notes: On the fixed explanation subsample for 2026-07, group G1_upstream_delay has the largest archived permutation MAE increase, 14.951 minutes, with repeat standard deviation 0.097 over 5 repeats. This explains the retained learned model separately from a potentially winning baseline. Joint-group permutation preserves within-group relationships but may break relationships across groups. Repeat standard deviation is not a confidence interval. Group permutation changes cannot be added together or substituted for staged feature increments. PDP uses hypothetical input replacements that may leave observed correlated-feature support. Coefficients, importance and airport rankings therefore do not identify causal effects. The date-block intervals resample saved predictions with common date draws. They do not repeat training or selection, and they are not selection-adjusted. The evidence also covers one season, conditional completed chains and incomplete weather delivery provenance. NOAA supplementation is retrospective. Any change made after seeing August requires a genuinely new unseen evaluation period, rather than relabeling the same test as independent validation.

claims: RQ1: 25 supported estimates under frozen common support
RQ2: Random forest, final MAE 13.655 min
A new season is needed to test generalization
slides.notes: The airport answer is conditional on 25 supported final estimates and the frozen common reference. The prediction answer is the frozen Random forest predictor with August MAE 13.655 minutes. The useful next step is an independently evaluated new season with stronger availability evidence and explicit operational eligibility, while preserving the archived decisions and unsuccessful experiments.
